subject: Premium support packaging — uptime bands, on‑call credits, and warm‑standby options

3) Explain the "warm‑standby" option you mentioned vs a Dedicated pool (what's included, behaviour during sustained peaks, and price delta).

Procurement would like any discounts tied to an annual commit spelled out (and what triggers an overage). Security also asked for the questionnaire (attached).

Hi Erin —

Appreciate the clear asks. Below is a concise summary and a draft starting offer — I'll attach a formal quote as well. High level: we carve reliability into three composable pieces — uptime band, response ladder, and escalation retainer — so customers can mix and match by risk tolerance and budget.

1) Uptime bands and crediting (examples):
  • 99.9% — base hosted plan; credits = 10% of monthly invoice for incidents that lower monthly availability under the threshold.
  • 99.95% — mid band; credits = 20% of monthly invoice when breached.
  • 99.99% — premium; credits = 40% of monthly invoice for qualifying breaches.

2) Response ladder (time is from incident report):
  • P1 (critical): 1 hour acknowledged, 4 hour remediation target with 24/7 on‑call.
  • P2 (high): 4 hour acknowledged, 24 hour remediation target (business hours with extended on‑call).
  • P3 (normal): Next business day triage.

Definitions and examples are in the attached quote; we also include an on‑call escalation matrix (first triage, second on‑call engineer, third manager/SME).

3) Warm‑standby vs Dedicated pool:
  • Warm‑standby: reserved, partially provisioned capacity that can be scaled to full within a short warm‑up window (~15–60 minutes depending on model). Lower monthly cost than Dedicated; good for spiky workloads that accept brief capacity ramp.
  • Dedicated pool: always‑hot capacity for pinned throughput and the lowest latency variance. Higher monthly committed price but predictable performance during sustained peaks.

Pricing delta (example): warm‑standby ~ 40% of equivalent Dedicated reserved capacity monthly price; burst usage charged at a reduced overage rate.

Discounts for commit: 10% for 12‑month TCV commit; 15% for 24‑month. We can tier further for higher commit bands. Overage triggers are monthly token/embedding thresholds — unused committed consumption can be carried as "on‑bill credits" on a per‑quarter smoothing basis (we call this credit sculpting — it avoids losing committed value for predictable seasonality).

I've attached a draft quote (VIV‑Quote‑FH‑2025‑05.pdf) with two package options (Pilot + Premium Pilot Retainer, and Annual Uptime Pack w/ warm‑standby). Would you like us to walk procurement through the DocuSign/contract language?

Next step: If this looks directionally correct I can add Karthik for the technical comparison call and Laura for the contract language. Happy to hop on a 30m call tomorrow.

Thanks —

Thanks Vivek — this is helpful. A couple clarifying Qs from SRE and procurement after I skimmed the quote: 

1) "Credit sculpting" sounds promising — can you confirm the carry window? You wrote per‑quarter smoothing — does that mean unused committed capacity from April can offset May/June overages?
2) For P1: is the 4‑hour remediation a firm contractual target or a best‑effort SLO? We need to know for our internal incident playbooks.
3) Warm‑standby cost math: can you give an example for our expected peak (we typically have 6 hours/day of 3x baseline traffic during business hours with occasional 24h spikes). If warm‑standby requires a 15–60 minute warm up, that might be acceptable if the burst admission is handled cleanly without cascading token failures.

Also legal wants to understand the breach window calculation for credits (rolling 30 day vs calendar month).

Happy to have Karthik join for the technical breakdown. Can Karthik and someone from product ops show a short diagram of how warm‑standby behaves during ramp (eviction, cache coldness, KV restoration)?

—Erin

Hi Erin —

Quick technical notes to address your SRE points (pasting only the highlights; I can send a short ops diagram if helpful):

• "Credit sculpting": yes — "carry window" is per quarter by default. Unused committed capacity within a quarter can offset overage in the same quarter; for long tails we can extend to a 6‑month smoothing window by contract.

• P1 remediation: We treat 1h/4h as contractual SLOs tied to the retainer. Credits for failure are calculated monthly on a calendar‑month basis (not rolling 30 day) unless specifically negotiated. That makes credit calculations deterministic for billing systems.

• Warm‑standby behaviour: the warm pool keeps a lightweight process image with preloaded models and preallocated KV slots; on spike we rehydrate caches and spin up runtime instances. Typical coldness cost is increased latency for the first few minutes of a spike (we bake-in a short burst headroom to avoid immediate token failures). For your pattern (6 hours/day at 3x), warm‑standby with an added short burst buffer works well and is ~40% of dedicated cost.

Pricing example (illustrative):
  • Dedicated (reserved): $60k/mo for capacity X
  • Warm‑standby: $24k/mo + burst usage @ 30% of on‑demand per token rate.

If you want, I can prepare a one‑page ops diagram showing cache rehydration + fallback routing (model downgrade → cross‑region fallback → read‑only degraded responses). Attaching a small ops note that summarizes the differences.

—Karthik
